title: What can DRC’s national dialogue achieve?
gist: Chatham House argues DRC President Tshisekedi's 27 August national dialogue — pitched as a 26-province process to 're-found' the state — is in practice likely to legitimize a post-2028 transition of three to five years, amid tacit government-opposition agreement that 2028 elections cannot happen and a controversial bill targeting constitutional article 220 on term limits. With a fragmented opposition, US backing after a critical minerals deal and the churches still undecided, Tshisekedi holds the stronger hand, and the main risk is an elite power-sharing deal echoing Kabila's 2016-17 'glissement' while the Washington, Doha and domestic peace tracks remain interdependent.

themes.theme: Tshisekedi's re-founding dialogue vs opposition rejection

insights.claim: DRC President Félix Tshisekedi announced a 'national dialogue' on 27 August 2026 built on public consultations in all 26 provinces culminating in a Kinshasa convention, with the stated aim not just of addressing insecurity and inequality but of reconstructing or 're-founding' the Congolese state.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A state 're-founding' agenda signals potential constitutional and institutional rewrites that could alter the legal framework under which DRC mining contracts and licences operate.

insights.claim: The DRC opposition C64 coalition (Moïse Katumbi, Martin Fayulu, Delly Sesanga, Jean-Marc Kabund) and exiled ex-president Joseph Kabila's 'Sauvons le Congo' platform both rejected Tshisekedi's national dialogue as a vehicle to legitimize changing the constitution and extending his rule beyond the two-term limit ending in 2028.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Broad, cross-faction opposition rejection raises the odds of a contested legitimacy crisis around 2028 — a key political-risk input for DRC-exposed copper/cobalt names.

insights.claim: A controversial DRC bill would pave the way for a referendum to modify article 220 of the constitution, the clause that forbids changing the number or duration of presidential terms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Progress of the article 220 referendum bill is the single clearest trackable milestone for a Tshisekedi term extension.
insights.quote: a controversial bill that would pave the way for a referendum allowing the modification of article 220 of the constitution

insights.claim: Tshisekedi's government and the opposition hold fundamentally incompatible framings: the president blames DRC's crisis mainly on Rwanda's backing of M23, while much of the opposition and the Catholic and Protestant churches see the M23 conflict as a symptom of bad governance and corruption under Tshisekedi.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Without a shared diagnosis, the dialogue is unlikely to yield durable reform — price DRC governance risk as persistent rather than resolving.
insights.quote: the conflict is more a symptom of the political crisis than its cause

insights.claim: Tshisekedi is using the national dialogue to build a 'united front' under his own control aligned against Rwanda, while refusing to include M23 (reserving that for the Doha Process), ruling out a venue outside the DRC that would let exiled politicians attend, and relegating religious denominations to a secondary or symbolic role.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Design choices signal a president-controlled process rather than a genuine negotiation, raising the chance of a co-opted rather than consensual outcome.

insights.claim: Behind closed doors, both DRC's government and opposition acknowledge that elections probably cannot be held by the end of Tshisekedi's second term in 2028, creating broad but tacit agreement to delay elections in favour of 'dialogue'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investors should treat a missed 2028 election and an extra-constitutional transition as the base case, not a tail risk, in DRC political-risk models.
insights.quote: elections probably cannot be held by the end of Tshisekedi’s second term in 2028

insights.claim: Three factors make a 2028 DRC election unlikely: little organizational progress so election quality would be questionable; M23 holding important eastern territories, where excluding those provinces could be read as endorsing secession and country break-up; and some opposition figures seeing dialogue as a route to power without the polls.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Territorial control by M23 directly feeds constitutional timelines — escalation in the east lengthens the likely transition period.

insights.claim: Those close to Tshisekedi hope for broad agreement on a three-to-five-year post-2028 transition, which would amount to a de facto extension of his tenure beyond constitutional limits if he stayed in office throughout; some opposition figures instead want a shorter transition, possibly without Tshisekedi, via power-sharing, a new electoral commission and fresh elections.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Scenario tree for DRC to 2031-33: long Tshisekedi-led transition vs short power-sharing transition — the former implies policy continuity for mining partners like the US.

insights.claim: The prospective post-2028 transition in DRC echoes the two-year 'glissement' Joseph Kabila negotiated in 2016-17 to stay beyond his second term, and the core risk is that Tshisekedi uses talks to co-opt part of the opposition just as Kabila did.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The 2016-17 glissement is the historical template for how DRC term-overruns play out — use it to calibrate duration and unrest risk.
insights.quote: The risk is that he intends to use talks as a way of co-opting part of the opposition, just as Kabila did in 2016-17.

insights.claim: The DRC opposition wants to wrest power from Tshisekedi but does not necessarily favour elections to resolve the crisis, and may see dialogue as the best means of unseating the president — meaning neither side is genuinely committed to an electoral route.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Opposition victory would not necessarily mean a return to constitutional order; elite-bargain outcomes dominate either way.

insights.claim: The DRC opposition is fragmented, unable to shape the dialogue's terms and lacks popular-mobilization leverage — a long-postponed opposition rally on 15 September 2026 drew relatively little participation in Kinshasa.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Weak street mobilization lowers near-term unrest risk in the capital and supports continuity of the Tshisekedi government.

insights.claim: The US, which recently signed a critical minerals deal with the DRC, is seen as backing Tshisekedi, and a recent presidential ordinance laid the groundwork for the dialogue under his control, so the president seems likely to move ahead with his plan.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US critical-minerals alignment effectively underwrites the incumbent — positive for continuity of US-linked mining offtake, but ties Western supply chains to a regime heading beyond term limits.
insights.quote: the US, which recently signed a critical minerals deal with the DRC, is seen to be backing Tshisekedi

insights.claim: The Catholic and Protestant churches are the key swing actor: they have not commented publicly and are negotiating for a stronger role, but an active church boycott could diminish the dialogue's legitimacy — the Catholic church was instrumental in organizing against a Kabila third term.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch church statements as the leading indicator of whether the dialogue loses legitimacy and mass opposition becomes viable.
insights.quote: The Catholic church is an important political actor in the DRC

themes.theme: Eastern war tied to constitutional politics

insights.claim: Since late 2021 the Rwanda-backed M23 has seized large swathes of North and South Kivu, including the provincial capitals Goma and Bukavu.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Loss of eastern provincial capitals keeps the mineral-rich Kivus outside state control — a persistent supply-chain provenance risk for eastern DRC minerals.

insights.claim: Talk of changing the DRC constitution by Tshisekedi's camp waned in early 2025 after M23 seized Goma and Bukavu and resurged once the threat was contained, showing that eastern security and national politics move together.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Stabilization in the east may paradoxically raise domestic political risk by freeing the incumbent to pursue a constitutional change.
insights.quote: It resurged once the threat was contained.

insights.claim: DRC peace runs on three linked tracks — Washington for DRC-Rwanda negotiations, the Qatar-led Doha Process for DRC-M23 talks, and the national dialogue — and none can succeed alone: no M23 agreement can exist without an accord with Rwanda, and eastern peace needs transitional justice and community reconciliation that belong in the national dialogue.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Monitor the three tracks jointly; a breakdown in the Washington DRC-Rwanda track undermines the Doha and domestic tracks and any US-backed minerals corridor.
insights.quote: No agreement with the M23 can exist without an accord with Rwanda.

insights.claim: Chatham House judges the greatest risk of DRC's national dialogue is that it collapses into exactly what Tshisekedi said it must not be: an exercise in which political elites agree how and when power will change hands, rather than delivering reforms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect an elite power-sharing outcome with limited governance reform — little improvement in the corruption and governance drivers the opposition blames for M23's success.
insights.quote: to an exercise in which political elites agree how and when power will change hands
